name: Pleasure as the sole good (Epicurean hedonism)
plain_explanation: Epicurus held that pleasure is simply what makes life good, and pain is what makes it bad -- nothing else (honour, wealth, virtue for its own sake) matters except as a means to pleasure or the avoidance of pain.
precise_definition: The ethical doctrine that pleasure is the beginning and end of the good life, and that virtue, justice, wisdom, and culture have value only insofar as they serve or are 'referred to' the pursuit of pleasure and the avoidance of pain.
why_it_mattered: It is the foundation of the entire Epicurean ethical and physical system, and, revived essentially unchanged, becomes the basis of modern utilitarianism via Bentham.
historical_origin: Formulated by Epicurus in Athens from 307 B.C. onward and fixed, according to Russell, 'once for all' by its founder, unlike the continually developing doctrine of Stoicism.
examples: Epicurus's statement that he cannot conceive the good if the pleasures of taste, love, hearing, and sight are withdrawn
'The beginning and root of all good is the pleasure of the stomach; even wisdom and culture must be referred to this'
objections: Ancient critics (especially Stoics such as Epictetus) accused Epicureanism of being 'swinish' and lacking moral exaltation
competing_positions: Stoic ethics (Ch. XXVIII), which makes virtue, not pleasure, the sole good
influence_on_later_thinkers: Directly anticipates Jeremy Bentham's utilitarianism; Russell explicitly compares Epicurus to Bentham on both hedonism and inconsistency (both were kinder in practice than their egoistic theory strictly required).
connection_to_politics_or_religion: Leads Epicurus to advise withdrawal from public life, since political power invites envy and disturbs tranquility.
